inline.s: Like a city of gandharvas, like illusion, like water in a mirage,
Not existing yet seeming to exist—so too are dharmas of dependent arising.
Relying on three kinds of mind, I speak provisionally of faculties, objects, and self;
Yet those minds and consciousnesses have no self-nature whatsoever.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness—selfless, and of two kinds;
The five dharmas and self-nature are the realm of all the Buddhas.
Habit-energy is their single cause, and from it the three marks are formed;
As with a single color, one paints a wall and sees many things.
The five dharmas and the two selflessnesses, self-nature, mind, and consciousness—
Within the Buddha lineage, all of these are wholly unattainable.
Far removed from mind and consciousness, and apart from the five dharmas;
Apart again from self-nature—this is the Buddha lineage.
If by body, speech, and mind one cultivates not the pure white dharmas;
The Tathāgata’s pure lineage is then far from manifestation.
Sovereign in the powers of superknowledge, adorned by pure samādhi,
The various mind-born bodies—these are the Buddha’s pure lineage.
Inwardly self-realized and stainless, far removed from marks of cause,
The eighth ground and the Buddha ground are formed by the Tathāgata nature.
Far-going and Good Wisdom, the Dharma Cloud and the Buddha ground;
All these are the Buddha lineage; the rest are included in the two vehicles.
The Tathāgata’s mind is sovereign, yet for all the foolish folk,
Because the mind’s marks differ, he speaks of seven kinds of ground.
On the seventh ground there arise no faults of body, speech, or mind;
The eighth ground’s reliance is like a dream, like crossing a river.
The eighth ground and the fifth ground comprehend the crafts and sciences;
The Buddha’s sons can become kings among all that exist.
The wise do not discriminate whether born or not born,
Empty and non-empty, self-nature and no self-nature—
These are but measures of the mind, and truly unattainable.
For the two vehicles he teaches: this is real, this is false;
Not so for the Buddha’s sons—therefore one should not discriminate.
Existence and non-existence are both unreal, and no mark of an instant is found;
Conventional and real dharmas are likewise none—only mind, ungraspable.
Dharmas that exist are conventional truth; the absence of nature is the supreme meaning;
To be deluded about that absence of nature—this is the worldly view.
All dharmas are empty; for the common and the foolish,
I set them forth provisionally, following the world—yet these have no reality.
The dharmas that arise from words have meanings they seem to convey;
But seeing what words give rise to, one finds it all unattainable.
As without a wall there is no painting, without substance no shadow;
If the storehouse consciousness is pure, the waves of the consciousnesses do not arise.
From the dharmakāya there is the reward body; from the reward arises the emanation body;
This is the root Buddha; all others are what emanation manifests.
One should not falsely discriminate emptiness and non-emptiness;
Falsely reckoning existence and non-existence, the meaning of words is unattainable.
The common and foolish falsely discriminate the real qualities of atoms gathered into form;
Each and every atom is none—therefore there is no object.
The outer marks that beings see are all manifested by their own minds;
Since what is seen does not exist, there are no outer objects at all.
Like an elephant sunk in deep mud, unable to move again;
The śrāvaka abiding in samādhi is mired and bogged just the same.
If one sees the world with habit-energy as its cause;
Beyond existence, non-existence, and both—in the selflessness of dharmas there is release.
Imagined nature is false reckoning; dependent arising is the other-dependent;
Suchness is the perfected—this I constantly teach in my sutras.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness, discrimination and expression;
The root consciousness makes the three realms—all are other names for mind.
Lifespan, warmth, and consciousness, ālaya and the life faculty;
Intellect and consciousness—all are other names for discrimination.
The mind can sustain the body; the intellect ever weighs and ponders;
Consciousness together with all the consciousnesses cognizes the mind’s own object.
If a self truly existed, apart from the skandhas or within them;
Seeking that self there, one finds it utterly unattainable.
Observe the world one by one: it is all one’s own mind appearing;
From the afflictions and their latency, one is freed from suffering and released.
The śrāvaka has the wisdom of exhaustion; the pratyekabuddha, the wisdom of stillness;
The Tathāgata’s wisdom arises without end or limit.
Outwardly there is truly no form—it is only what one’s own mind manifests;
The foolish do not know this, and falsely discriminate the conditioned.
Not knowing that outer objects of every kind are all one’s own mind;
The foolish establish them by reasons and analogies, through the four propositions.
The wise fully comprehend that objects are one’s own mind appearing;
They do not establish them by tenets, reasons, analogies, or any propositions.
Discrimination and the discriminated—this is the mark of false reckoning;
Resting upon false reckoning, discrimination arises once again.
They lean on one another in turn, all from a single habit-energy;
These two are both but guests; they do not arise from beings’ minds.
Dwelling at ease within the three realms, mind and mental factors discriminate;
The seeming objects that arise are the imagined self-nature.
Images and seeds together make the twelve sense-fields;
When support and object join, one speaks of deeds that are performed.
Like an image in a mirror, like hairs seen by a clouded eye;
So too when habit-energy covers, ordinary folk give rise to false views.
Toward the objects of one’s own discrimination, discrimination then arises;
As the sectarians discriminate—outer objects are unattainable.
As the fool, not knowing a rope, seizes it falsely as a snake;
Not knowing the mind’s own appearing, he falsely discriminates outer objects.
Thus the rope’s own body is apart from both sameness and difference;
It is only the mind’s inverted delusion that falsely raises the rope-discrimination.
When one falsely reckons and discriminates, that nature is not there;
How is it that, seeing what is not, discrimination arises?
The nature of form is nothing at all, and so are pot and cloth;
They arise only from discrimination; what is seen in the end does not exist."
"Amid beginningless conditioned existence, confusion gives rise to discrimination;
What dharma causes the confusion? May the Buddha speak it for me."
"All dharmas have no self-nature; they are only what the mind manifests;
Not comprehending one’s own mind, one therefore gives rise to discrimination.
As the foolish discriminate and falsely reckon, it truly does not exist;
What exists otherwise than this, they are unable to know.
What the noble ones possess is not what the foolish discriminate;
If the noble were the same as the common, the noble would have falsity.
Because the noble one governs and purifies the mind, there is no confusion;
The common and foolish mind is impure, and so false discrimination arises.
As a mother speaks to her infant: you need not weep and wail;
Fruits will come down from the sky, and you may take them, all kinds, as you please.
For beings I teach the fruits of every kind of false reckoning;
Having made them love and delight in it, the Dharma truly transcends existence and non-existence.
All dharmas were at first non-existent, their conditions not yet joined;
What was unborn appears as born, and has no self-nature at all.
An unborn dharma does not arise; apart from conditions there is no place of birth;
So too with dharmas now arising—apart from conditions they are unattainable.
Observing the essential truth of dependent arising: neither existing nor not existing;
Not existing, not non-existing, not both—the wise do not discriminate.
The foolish folk among the sectarians falsely speak of sameness and difference;
They do not comprehend dependent arising: the world is like illusion, like a dream.
My unsurpassed Great Vehicle transcends words and names;
Its meaning is most clear, yet the foolish do not awaken to it.
What the śrāvakas and sectarians teach is all stingy and withheld;
They make the meaning all distorted—all of it arising from false reckoning.
All marks and self-bodies, their shapes and their names—
